title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
description: Separate configuration from code using ConfigMaps and manage sensitive data securely with Kubernetes Secrets, following the twelve-factor app methodology.

data.text: The **twelve-factor app** methodology states that configuration should be strictly separated from code. In Kubernetes, **ConfigMaps** and **Secrets** fulfill this requirement. ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs, while Secrets store sensitive data such as passwords, OAuth tokens, and TLS certificates.

Both ConfigMaps and Secrets can be injected into Pods as environment variables, mounted as files in volumes, or used directly in command arguments. This means you can change configuration without rebuilding container images.

terms.definition: A Kubernetes object for storing non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs.
A Kubernetes object for storing sensitive data; values are base64-encoded by default.
Mounting ConfigMap or Secret data as files inside a container's filesystem.
Injecting ConfigMap or Secret values as env vars in a container.
Encrypting Secret data at rest in the Kubernetes cluster store.

data.text: ConfigMaps let you decouple configuration from container images. You define your configuration once in a ConfigMap, and multiple Pods can consume it. This is especially useful for feature flags, log levels, external service URLs, or any value that changes between environments (development, staging, production).

data.title: Creating a ConfigMap
data.content: Define application configuration in a ConfigMap.
data.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  API_URL: "https://api.production.example.com"
  TIMEOUT_SECONDS: "30"
  FEATURE_NEW_UI: "true"

data.title: Injecting ConfigMap as environment variables
data.content: Consume ConfigMap values inside a container as environment variables.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: myapp:2.0
        env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: LOG_LEVEL
        - name: API_URL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: API_URL

data.text: Secrets store sensitive data like database passwords, API keys, and TLS certificates. By default, Kubernetes stores Secret values as base64-encoded strings in etcd — **not encrypted**. You must enable encryption at rest in your cluster to protect Secrets from being read by someone with etcd access. Secrets also integrate with RBAC so you can control which users and Pods can read them.

data.title: Creating a database Secret
data.content: Store database credentials in a Kubernetes Secret.
data.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
type: Opaque
data:
  username: YWRtaW4=
  password: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=

data.title: Creating a Secret from the CLI
data.content: Use kubectl to create and inspect Secrets without manually encoding values.
data.code:
# Create a Secret from literal values
kubectl create secret generic db-secret \
  --from-literal=username=admin \
  --from-literal=password=secret123

# Decode to verify
echo 'cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=' | base64 --decode

data.title: Secrets are not encrypted by default
data.text: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Enable etcd encryption at rest in your cluster configuration, use RBAC to limit Secret access, and consider external secret managers like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager for production.

data.title: Manage configuration and secrets
data.description: Create ConfigMaps and Secrets and inject them into a running application.
steps: Create a ConfigMap named "app-config" with LOG_LEVEL and API_URL.
Create a Secret named "db-secret" with username and password.
Deploy an application that reads LOG_LEVEL from the ConfigMap and DB_PASSWORD from the Secret.
Mount the ConfigMap as a volume at /etc/config and the Secret at /etc/secrets.
Verify the files are present inside the container.
Update the ConfigMap and observe the change (if using volume mounts with updates).
data.expectedOutcome: Your application reads configuration from ConfigMaps and sensitive values from Secrets without hardcoding anything.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: ConfigMaps externalize non-sensitive configuration so you can change values without rebuilding images.
Secrets store sensitive data; enable etcd encryption at rest for true security.
Both ConfigMaps and Secrets can be injected as environment variables or mounted as volumes.
Secrets integrate with RBAC so only authorized workloads and users can access them.
Consider external secret managers for production-grade secrets management.
data.takeaway: Keep configuration and secrets out of your images — use ConfigMaps and Secrets to manage them dynamically.
